title: Vote for Me (Here's Why)
hook: A comment card about safety may be campaigning for a parking space.
counterintuition: A reason can be true and still be campaigning. In public, it explains a position while recruiting an audience; miss that audience, and you answer the words while the real campaign keeps moving.
tryThisNow: Before replying to one argument today, name the audience the speaker seems to be persuading, even if you are the only visible listener.
keyTakeaway: Ask what a reason is selling and whom it is recruiting before treating it as a private explanation of belief.

breakdown.fastRead:
A stack of comment cards leans against a cracked microphone base. Megan reads safety over and over in the zoning hearing file, but the zoning map tells another story. The safest streets named on the cards are also the streets where residents would lose parking.

She does not call the neighbors liars. She sorts the cards by audience. Some reassure parents. Some signal to homeowners. Some tell council members, I am the kind of person who protects this block.

A reason often behaves like a campaign handbill for the side already chosen.
breakdown.deepRead:
You see the investor deck and the all-hands notes open on the same laptop. Daniel has to explain a startup pivot before Friday. In the investor version, the reason is market discipline. In the employee version, the reason is sharper focus. Both are partly true. One protects credibility with money. The other protects trust inside the room.

Public reasons are rarely only mirrors. They are tools people use to gather allies, preserve reputation, and make a position easier to join.

That can sound cynical. It should not. Human beings reason in groups because moral life happens in groups. A public reason has to survive other people's eyes. It has to tell listeners what kind of person the speaker is and what kind of team they are invited to become.

The trick is to hear the invitation.

When Catarina taps the wage table in a union hall and says nobody chants a spreadsheet, she is not rejecting numbers. She is asking which sentence will make a wavering member feel seen by the group. The technical argument can calculate the loss. The loyalty argument can turn a lonely no into a shared no.

The guardrail is truth. If the recruiting sentence hides the numbers, it has become manipulation. If it carries the numbers into a group identity people can stand inside, it is doing the social work every public reason has to do.
breakdown.fullRead:
The receipt printer spits out a test check with the new service charge circled. Olivier stands beside the manager while the menu note sits unfinished. The guest-facing reason says transparency. The staff-facing reason says dignity, predictable pay, and no more smiling through a table's moral judgment. Olivier asks the manager to say the staff reason aloud before writing the menu note.

Once an argument enters a room with other people, the reason starts doing reputation work as well as truth work. It tells guests what kind of restaurant this wants to be. It tells servers whether management sees them as professionals or as costs. It tells owners whether they are brave enough to carry the policy in public.

Which audience is your reason trying hardest to impress?

Devon learned the cost of missing the audience on a porch. His school board fact sheet answered a curriculum rumor cleanly and lost anyway. Parents did not hear correction. They heard contempt. After one canvassing shift, he marked the sentence that would recruit anxious parents instead of humiliating them. The facts stayed. The posture changed.

This is the social persuasion framing at its honest edge. A reason that recruits can still be true. A reason that protects reputation can still be fair. The failure comes when the recruiting job is hidden, because then everyone pretends the argument is only about evidence while the audience is being chosen in the background.

Anya sees the same pressure in a research lab after a failed replication. Her draft statement names the replication file and the journal email, but one sentence tells the truth and another campaigns for the lab. She asks which sentence she would keep if nobody knew her name was on the paper. That question does not remove reputation. It reveals where reputation has touched the draft.

Vote for Me (Here's Why) is not only a political move. It is what many public reasons whisper: join my side, trust my kind of person, let my group remain respectable. If you hear only the literal claim, you miss the social work. If you hear the social work, you can answer with more accuracy and less surprise.

The practical move is not to accuse everyone of bad faith. It is to ask what the reason is doing in the room. Is it making a claim easier to test, or making a tribe easier to join? Is it naming a real value, or hiding a status play behind a value word? Those questions let you stay fair without becoming naive.

A public reason lives in two places at once. It lives in the evidence it names, and it lives in the audience it gathers. Good judgment listens to both places before replying.

That double listening changes the reply. You can answer the evidence without insulting the audience. You can challenge the campaign without pretending the stated reason is fake. The point is sharper response, not cynicism.

examples.title: Megan Sorts the Comment Cards

planSpec.domain: city zoning hearing where neighbors cite safety to protect parking
planSpec.audience: planners reading moral rhetoric in public comments
planSpec.stakes: Megan maps each stated reason to the constituency it reassures.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Megan groups comment cards by the audience they signal to, not by the literal topic line.

examples.scenario: A stack of comment cards leans against a cracked microphone base in the planning office after a zoning hearing. Megan has the zoning map open beside them. Most cards say safety, but the red marks cluster where parking would disappear. Before she briefs council, she must decide whether to summarize the literal reasons or group the cards by the audience each reason reassures.
examples.whatToDo: Sort the cards by the constituency they signal to: parents, homeowners, commuters, or council members. Then answer both the safety claim and the parking campaign underneath it.
examples.whyItMatters: The word safety may be sincere and still be recruiting allies for another loss. Megan hears the argument better when she hears its audience.

examples.title: Daniel Circles the Status Sentence

planSpec.domain: startup founder explaining a pivot to employees and investors
planSpec.stakes: Daniel separates the reason that persuades staff from the reason that reassures investors.
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Daniel draft two versions and circle the sentence that protects his status more than the truth.

examples.scenario: You see the investor deck and the all-hands notes open on the same laptop in a startup conference room. Daniel has a runway chart in one tab and a draft pivot message in another. The investor line says discipline. The staff line says focus. One sentence, about always seeing the market early, protects his status more than the truth. Before Friday, he has to decide whether to keep it.
examples.whatToDo: Circle the status-saving sentence and cut it. Keep separate reasons for investors and staff, but make each one carry truth instead of vanity.
examples.whyItMatters: Different audiences need different explanations. The danger is letting reputation sneak into the reason and pretend it is evidence.

examples.title: Catarina Rewrites the Wage Argument

planSpec.domain: union local choosing language for a contract rejection
planSpec.stakes: Catarina rewrites a technical wage argument as a loyalty appeal to members.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Catarina asks which sentence will make a wavering member feel seen by the group.

examples.scenario: "Nobody chants a spreadsheet," Catarina says, tapping the wage table under the union hall lectern. The first flyer explains the contract gap in percentages. The second says a no vote tells part-time members they are not alone. Folded flyers sit in stacks by the door. Catarina asks which sentence will make a wavering member feel seen by the group.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the wage table, but lead with the loyalty sentence. Let the technical reason support the shared reason members can carry together.
examples.whyItMatters: The contract argument needs numbers and belonging. A public reason recruits action only when members can hear themselves inside it.

examples.title: Devon Marks the Porch Sentence

planSpec.domain: school board candidate responding to a curriculum rumor
planSpec.audience: campaign volunteers tempted by fact dumps
planSpec.stakes: Devon hears the reply as an audition for trust, not only an answer to a rumor.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Devon marks which sentence would recruit anxious parents instead of humiliating them.

examples.scenario: It took Devon one rainy canvassing shift on Maple Avenue to see that the fact sheet was losing the porch. The door hanger corrected the curriculum rumor, but the porch light stayed on over parents who felt mocked. Back at school-board headquarters, he marked the sentence that sounded like a scold and wrote one that would recruit anxious parents instead of humiliating them.
examples.whatToDo: Answer the rumor without performing superiority. Write the first sentence for anxious parents who need a way to join you without losing face.
examples.whyItMatters: A correction can be accurate and socially useless. Devon needs a reason that persuades the audience in front of him, not a fact sheet that flatters volunteers.

examples.title: Olivier Tests the Staff Reason

planSpec.domain: restaurant group defending a service charge policy
planSpec.stakes: Olivier identifies which reason is for guests and which is for staff pride.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Olivier asks the manager to say the staff-facing reason aloud before writing the menu note.

examples.scenario: The receipt printer spits out a test check with the new service charge circled before the 5 p.m. dinner briefing. "Guests will want transparency," the manager says, menu note open beside the printer. Olivier points to the line cooks visible through the pass. "Say the staff reason aloud first." Before service, he has to decide which reason belongs on the menu and which belongs in the staff meeting.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the audiences. Write guests a clear menu note, then tell staff the dignity and pay-stability reason without hiding behind guest transparency.
examples.whyItMatters: One policy speaks to two rooms. Olivier weakens both if he uses a guest reason to avoid saying the staff reason plainly.

examples.title: Anya Questions the Draft Statement

planSpec.domain: research lab deciding how to announce a failed replication
planSpec.stakes: Anya distinguishes the public reason from the status-saving reason in the draft statement.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Which sentence in Anya's draft tells the truth, and which one is campaigning for the lab?

examples.scenario: Which sentence would you keep if nobody knew your name was on the paper? Anya has the draft statement, the replication file, and the journal email open after midnight in the lab. One sentence says the finding did not replicate. Another says the lab has always modeled transparency. Before sending, she has to decide which sentence tells truth and which one campaigns for the lab.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the sentence that tells what happened and revise the sentence that flatters the lab. Let reputation be a constraint, not the hidden author.
examples.whyItMatters: The announcement must persuade peers, but persuasion should not turn a failed replication into a status performance.

questions.prompt: After a zoning hearing, a city planning file repeats safety language, but the comment cards cluster around streets that would lose parking. What should the planner listen for?
choices: Which audience the safety reason is trying to reassure or recruit.
Whether residents are lying about every safety concern.
Whether parking should be ignored because safety sounds nobler.
questions.explanation: The safety concern may be real, but it is also doing public work. The planner should hear both the literal claim and the constituency it gathers.

questions.prompt: In a startup conference room, a founder writes two pivot explanations, one for investors and one for employees, and one sentence mainly protects his status. Which edit best protects truth?
choices: Use the investor language everywhere so the message stays consistent.
Cut the sentence that mainly protects his status while keeping audience-specific truthful reasons.
Tell employees nothing until the market story is final.
questions.explanation: Different audiences can need different reasons. The problem is the vanity sentence that recruits trust by rewriting the founder's status.

questions.prompt: A union flyer explains a contract gap with percentages, but wavering members do not repeat it. What stronger move should the organizer make?
choices: Remove all numbers because solidarity cannot use evidence.
Print more copies of the same table.
Add a loyalty sentence members can carry together, with the table as support.
questions.explanation: The numbers matter, but they are not enough to recruit collective action. A public reason must give members language for belonging as well as calculation.

questions.prompt: A candidate's fact sheet corrects a rumor but makes anxious parents feel stupid. Which revision best fits the persuasion frame?
choices: Open with a sentence that respects the worry, then correct the false claim.
Double the number of facts so the error becomes undeniable.
Mock the rumor gently so supporters feel energized.
questions.explanation: The reply has to recruit anxious parents, not humiliate them. More facts or mockery may satisfy supporters while losing the intended audience.

questions.prompt: A restaurant owner defends a service charge to guests as transparency, but staff hear no mention of pay dignity. What should the owner do?
choices: Use only the guest reason because staff already understand the policy.
Drop the charge because one policy cannot have two audiences.
Give guests a clear fee note and staff a direct reason about dignity and stable pay.
questions.explanation: The same policy speaks to two rooms. Separating the audiences lets each reason do honest work instead of hiding staff pride behind guest language.

questions.prompt: A lab statement after a failed replication includes one plain sentence about the result and one glowing sentence about the lab's integrity. What is the deeper risk?
choices: The integrity sentence may be doing reputation work that competes with the truth-telling job.
The lab should never explain its values in public.
The failed replication should be kept private until reputation is safe.
questions.explanation: The issue is not that reputation exists. The risk is letting reputation write the statement while pretending the draft is only about the result.

questions.prompt: At a neighborhood forum, a speaker answers your question while staring at the television camera and the supporters in the back row. The reason sounds less aimed at you than at bystanders in the room. What should you analyze first?
choices: Whether the bystanders are morally weaker than the speaker.
How the reason helps the speaker recruit allies or preserve identity.
Whether the reason contains any long words.
questions.explanation: Public reasons often address the visible audience and the imagined one. The useful analysis is the social job the reason performs.

questions.prompt: A manager claims a policy is about fairness only after employees accuse leadership of protecting its image. What should you check?
choices: Whether fairness explains the policy even when reputation pressure is removed.
Whether employees should be banned from questioning motives.
Whether fairness language always proves hypocrisy.
questions.explanation: A reason can be true and still serve reputation. Testing the claim away from status pressure shows whether it is explanation or cover.

questions.prompt: A civic organizer can write a technically perfect answer or a slightly warmer answer that lets skeptical neighbors join without losing face. Which is stronger?
choices: The technical answer, because persuasion corrupts every argument.
Neither, because skeptical neighbors cannot be persuaded.
The warmer answer, if it stays truthful, because public reasons must recruit an audience.
questions.explanation: Truth still matters, but public reasoning also has to invite people into a position. The warmer answer works only if it keeps the facts intact.

reviewCards.front: A reason is spoken in public. What should you ask besides whether it is true?
reviewCards.back: Ask what it is selling and whom it is recruiting. Public reasons explain, but they also gather allies and protect reputation.

reviewCards.front: A technically correct argument loses the room. What may be missing?
reviewCards.back: It may fail to speak to the audience's identity, fear, loyalty, or need for dignity. A public reason must be true and socially legible.

reviewCards.front: How can reputation hide inside a moral argument?
reviewCards.back: A speaker may choose reasons that preserve status while presenting them as neutral explanation. Look for the sentence that mainly says, trust my kind of person.

reviewCards.front: A message has one audience in the room and another outside it. What is the move?
reviewCards.back: Separate the audiences. Name what each reason is doing for each group, then remove any line that flatters one group while pretending to explain to another.

reviewCards.front: Why is persuasion not automatically manipulation?
reviewCards.back: Reasoning is social. A truthful reason can still be shaped for an audience. The ethical question is whether the reason recruits honestly or hides its real job.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to hear the campaign inside a reason. Before answering the literal claim, identify the audience it is reassuring, recruiting, or protecting.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a reason sounds unusually noble in public, then ask which audience that nobility is trying to gather.
If you draft an explanation for two audiences, then mark which sentence is truth and which sentence is reputation management.
If a correction is accurate but alienating, then rewrite the first sentence so the intended audience can join without humiliation.
If someone gives a reason while allies are watching, then answer both the stated claim and the group signal it carries.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before replying to one argument today, write down the audience the speaker seems to be recruiting. Then draft your response for that audience too.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, collect three public reasons from work, civic life, or family. For each, label the stated claim, the intended audience, and the reputation the reason protects.

memorableLines.text: A reason often behaves like a campaign handbill for the side already chosen.
memorableLines.why: It lands the chapter's source anchor in a concrete political image without becoming partisan.

memorableLines.text: The trick is to hear the invitation.
memorableLines.why: The short line turns persuasion analysis into a memorable listening skill.

memorableLines.text: If you hear the social work, you can answer with more accuracy and less surprise.
memorableLines.why: It gives the payoff: better response, not cynicism about motives.
